title: Responsibility for identifying which contracts are in scope is non-delegable, even when third-party data determines the answer
content:
The smart-contract capital calculation begins with a scoping judgment, not a formula. A.3.2.2.1.2.1.1 requires identifying "all relevant smart contracts" — "those that are critical for the project being invested in, including core business logic, vaults, token contracts, and proxy implementations" — and A.3.2.2.1.2.1.2 requires obtaining verified source for the deployed version of each from a block explorer, "including any dependencies or inherited library contracts that are part of the live system."

Every downstream number depends on that set. Total lines of code, cyclomatic complexity, external calls, inheritance depth, audit coverage as a fraction of total lines, average contract age, and TVL are all computed *over the covered contracts*. A narrower scope mechanically lowers complexity and raises apparent audit coverage — the metrics reward under-scoping.

A.3.2.2.1.2.1.1.1 places the resulting risk squarely: external sources "such as third party data providers, security consultants, and project documentation may be used to help identify relevant smart contracts. However, the Prime Agent deploying funds from the Collateral Portfolio into the opportunity retains overall responsibility for the reasonableness of identifying the relevant smart contracts."

This is the necessary complement to a mechanically computed rating. Once complexity and audit metrics are formulas, the only remaining lever is the input set, so the framework's integrity rests on the scoping being honest. Rather than specifying scope exhaustively — impossible across arbitrary protocols — the Atlas assigns liability for the judgment and makes the standard "reasonableness," which is reviewable after the fact.

The pattern is worth naming: where a rule can be gamed only through a judgment that cannot be fully specified, the Atlas permits reliance on experts but refuses to let reliance transfer responsibility.
description: Agents may use data providers, security consultants and project documentation to scope relevant contracts, but retain overall responsibility for the reasonableness of that scoping.
